title: Paper curation memo — Context stitching, soft prefixes, and long-run inference heuristics
content:
Purpose and audience:
A compact curation of recent approaches and quick experiment ideas for long-context inference that I want to try on Redwood Dedicated during a low-traffic window. Intended for myself + Leah/Omar as a living memo. Not polished; think of it as a lab notebook + prioritized todo list.

High-level motivation (1-liner):
We need pragmatic techniques to let real products (assistants, copilots) maintain coherent state across tens of thousands of tokens without blowing latency or memory budgets. This is about making tradeoffs: when to stitch, when to compress, when to fall back.

Quick takeaways from papers/blogs I skimmed (snippets):
- "Context Stitching" idea (inspired by a few workshop talks): chunk a long history into semantically aligned windows, compute compressed representations per chunk, and let generation pull in k-nearest chunks as soft-context rather than concatenating raw tokens.
  - pro: reduces sequence length to model at runtime, can be combined with embedding-based retrieval.
  - cons: alignment mismatch, requires good chunking and prompt scaffolding to avoid hallucination.

- Soft-prefix tuning + adapter combos (various recent small papers): prepended continuous tokens (learned) act as a compact, parameterized context that steers behavior. Useful for: persona, long-term memory summaries, and compacting prompts. Can be cheaply cached per-user and applied at runtime with minimal token overhead.

- KV-cache compression techniques (arXiv preprints + internal Slack thread): lossy compression of past KV pairs (quantization, PCA, learned downprojection) to reduce GPU memory while preserving generation quality for long contexts. Key trick: compress only older layers or older timesteps, keep recent steps uncompressed.

- Chunk-level reranking / canonicalization: rather than relying on raw retrieval score, do a cheap re-score by sending top-n chunks through a small reranker model that estimates helpfulness to next-token prediction (proxy: log-prob delta on a short probe).

Concrete experiments to run (priority ordering):
1) Retrieval-as-soft-context prototype (high priority, quick):
   - Mechanism: chunk user history into 2k-token chunks; compute chunk embeddings (we already have an embed endpoint); at request time retrieve top-3 chunks, serialize each chunk as a short natural-language summary using a small summarizer (200 tokens) or use learned soft-prefix representation. Feed summaries + short deltas (recent 512 tokens) into model.
   - Metrics: latency P50/P95, end-to-end token cost, and QA/rollout fidelity on a held-out set of dialogues (we'll re-use the SQuAD-style probes from the eval harness).
   - Risks: hallucination from summary drift; evaluate with calibrated QA checks.

2) KV-cache progressive compression (medium priority):
   - Start with existing KV cache snapshot of a 13B-style model running at 8k steps; implement simple PCA downprojection of keys/values every time we cross a chunk boundary (e.g., every 1024 tokens). Compare naive quantization (8-bit) vs PCA(64) vs learned projection (tiny MLP).
   - Measure: memory usage and generation perplexity on continuation tasks; manual check for prompt-completion consistency.
   - Implementation note: stash small metadata to allow decompression/denoising on read.

3) Soft-prefix per-user prototypes (lower effort, high payoff for personalization):
   - Train a 256-token soft-prefix per user on short context windows (fine-tune or adapt via adapter). Store prefixes in dedicated KV store keyed by user-id. At inference, prepend prefix tokens (treated as virtual tokens).
   - Evaluate: personalization coherency (user-specific preferences maintained), cost amortization, and effect on latency.

4) Chunk reranker integration (quick experiment):
   - Pipeline: retrieval -> small reranker (100M) -> assemble top-2 chunks + recent context -> generation. Reranker objective: estimated delta in next-token log-prob on probe.
   - Evaluate quality improvements vs latency hit.

Practical heuristics and runtime policies (sketch):
- Age-based strategy: perform lossy compression on chunks older than M tokens where M is dynamic based on current request latency SLO. If under SLO slack, decompress extra chunks.
- Fidelity gates: run a cheap detector that predicts if the user query needs exact context (e.g., "account balance" or legal text). For high-fidelity queries, bypass compression and join more raw tokens.
- Multi-tier model routing: small model + compressed context for cheap queries; larger model + raw context for high-criticality queries. Redwood routing layer should be able to express this policy.

Notes on evaluation datasets (quick plan):
- Use a mixture of internal dialogue traces (anonymized) + synthetic long-context tests:
  - Persona consistency tasks (does assistant remember earlier claims)
  - Retrieval QA style probes spread across history (needle-in-haystack facts)
  - Long-form summarization continuity (generate accurate multi-section summaries)
- Create a short eval harness (10–15 inputs per scenario) that can be run as a smoke test during nightly runs.

Implementation TODOs (who/approx time):
- [Kai] Prototype retrieval-as-soft-context pipeline (2–3 days). Need helper code to chunk histories + summarize with small model.
- [Leah] Wire up embedding persistence and retrieval latency measurement (1 day).
- [Omar] Add PCA-quant compression op to runtime memory layer and a toggle in the dev console (2–3 days).
- [Kai + Omar] Plan a micro-benchmark run on Dedicated dev cluster; schedule during maintenance window.

Open questions / design tradeoffs (brain-dump):
- How to avoid the silent drift/hallucination problem when summaries or compressed KVs lose precise referents? Possible mitigation: include provenance tokens (chunk-id markers) and a cheap citation mechanism so model can say "I might be recalling from chunk #5".
- How aggressive can compression be before downstream hallucination rises sharply? Need a knee-plot (compression ratio vs emulated QA accuracy).
- Runtime complexity: decompress-on-demand adds tail latency — is it better to over-provision memory for cold shards or pay occasional decompression cost?

References and quick links (for later reading):
- paper: "Long Context Compression for Transformer KV Caches" (arXiv 2027) — focuses on layer-wise compression. (see linked artifacts above)
- blog: "Soft Prefixing for Few-shot Personalization" — practical recipes, code snippets.
- infra note: internal Confluence page for "kv-cache-compression-proto" (link above).

Short-term acceptance criteria for pushing an A/B: if retrieval-as-soft-context reduces tokenized input length by >= 40% and end-to-end quality (QA probe) drops <= 3% absolute, promote to canary with 5% traffic. If hallucination rate increases > 5% absolute, roll back.

Final micro-remarks (quick and dirty):
- Keep this memo alive; will update after first prototype run.
- If anyone else wants to try a variant (e.g., learned chunking boundaries via a tiny model), ping and I'll add to the sheet.

Next steps: implement the chunking + summarizer sketch, and assemble a 20-example eval set.
